**Editor's Note:** Reese Witherspoon, the Academy Award-winning actress, serves as honorary chairman of the Avon Foundation and is employed by Avon Products as its global ambassador. In the following piece, Reese Witherspoon expresses her determination to dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer.

**(CNN)** -- Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic terrifying. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing this figure put everything into perspective.

Women close to me have battled the disease and now stand as soldiers in the greater fight against it. Yet the moment I heard "every three minutes," I felt vulnerable and afraid, suddenly realizing that no one is immune. The only way to ease my fears was to take action. I needed to educate both myself and others about this disease.

As the Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation, I had valuable resources at my fingertips. I had access to an entire organization devoted to giving back to women and educating the public. So I began asking, "What do I need to know?" It was through that curiosity that I discovered the single most important fact about breast cancer: early detection saves lives.

According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, there is a 97 percent five-year survival rate when breast cancer is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body. When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is precisely why women must perform self-exams regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change.

Of course, discussing breast cancer and breast health is a deeply personal matter. I, too, am a private person, but I encourage all women to overcome their reservations and speak openly with their doctors and physicians.

We must also dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who had been diagnosed in their 20s—an age when most women are graduating from college and just beginning their lives as full adults. *Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »*

Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam performed by a health professional at least once every three years, and women 40 and older should have an exam every year.

I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for future generations of women, so that one day we will no longer have to live in fear of breast cancer. I began my fight by learning the important first steps in breast cancer detection, and I will not rest until every woman can stand together and declare that we are breast cancer free.

More than anything else, I have faith—faith that we will find a cure. I saw this commitment in the faces of the women in Washington: in the faces of those who walked, and in the faces of the women and men who stood on the sidelines, cheering the 3,500 participants toward the finish line. I was cheering right alongside them, calling out for action to find a cure.

Avon's next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

**Editor's Note:** Reese Witherspoon, an Oscar-winning actress, serves as honorary chairman of the Avon Foundation and works with Avon Products in the role of global ambassador. She hopes to dispel the misconception that breast cancer poses no threat to younger women.

(CNN) -- Somewhere in America, a woman receives a breast cancer diagnosis once every three minutes. Being a woman, a mother, and a daughter myself, I find that number absolutely chilling. Breast cancer was never something I ignored, but learning this figure gave me a whole new understanding of its reality.

Several women I care about have fought this illness and now stand as warriors in the broader campaign against it. Yet when I heard those words—"every three minutes"—I suddenly felt exposed and frightened, grasping that the disease can strike anyone. For me, the sole way to calm those fears was to do something about it. I had to become informed and help inform others.

Serving as Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation, I had tremendous resources within reach. An entire organization committed to supporting women and spreading awareness was available to me. So I began to ask, "What are the things I should understand?" That very curiosity led me to the single most crucial truth about breast cancer: catching it early can save a life.

The Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade reports that when the disease is detected before spreading elsewhere in the body, the five-year survival rate reaches 97 percent. In its earliest stages, breast cancer typically produces no warning signs, which is precisely why women should routinely examine themselves and reach out to their physician the instant they notice any change, however minor.

Naturally, discussing breast cancer and breast health can feel deeply personal. I consider myself a private person as well, but I urge every woman to move past her hesitations and speak openly with her doctors and medical providers.

We also need to put an end to the false belief that younger women face no risk of breast cancer. During the Avon Walk in Washington, I encountered young survivors who received their diagnosis while in their 20s—a time when most women are finishing college and just beginning adult life. Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »

Women in their 20s and 30s ought to receive a clinical breast examination performed by a health professional at minimum once every three years, while those aged 40 and up should be examined annually.

I feel deeply driven to combat this terrible disease. I fight on behalf of my mother, myself, my children, and the women of generations to come, so that someday breast cancer will no longer be something we dread. My fight started with learning the essential early steps of detecting breast cancer, and it won't stop until every woman can join together and declare that we are free of breast cancer.

Above all, I hold onto hope—hope that a cure lies ahead. I witnessed that same resolve in the expressions of the women in Washington, both those making the walk and the women and men lining the route, urging all 3,500 participants toward the finish. I was cheering alongside them, shouting for the action needed to discover a cure.

Avon's upcoming walk is scheduled for New York City on October 4 and 5.

# Understanding Breast Cancer: Awareness, Early Detection, and Advocacy

Every three minutes, a woman in the United States is diagnosed with breast cancer. This sobering statistic underscores a critical truth: anyone can be susceptible to the disease, regardless of age, lifestyle, or background. Understanding the realities of breast cancer is the first step toward protecting ourselves and the people we love.

Public figures have an important role to play in raising awareness. Reese Witherspoon, for example, uses her position as Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation to educate both herself and others about breast cancer. Her advocacy demonstrates how influential voices can help spread vital information and encourage people to take their health seriously.

One of the most important messages to communicate is that early detection saves lives. When breast cancer is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body, the five-year survival rate is an encouraging 97 percent. This remarkable statistic highlights why vigilance and timely medical attention are so essential.

Because breast cancer usually presents no early symptoms, women cannot rely on warning signs alone to alert them to a problem. Instead, they should perform regular self-examinations and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change. Proactive self-awareness can make all the difference in identifying the disease at its most treatable stage.

Finally, we must banish the dangerous myth that young women are not at risk. Some survivors were diagnosed in their 20s, proving that breast cancer does not discriminate by age. By dispelling this misconception, we empower women of all ages to stay informed, remain attentive to their bodies, and seek care when something seems wrong.

# Understanding the Threat of Breast Cancer

Breast cancer poses a serious threat to all women, cutting across every demographic and defying many of the assumptions people hold about who is truly at risk. Too often, young women are mistakenly considered low-risk, leading them to overlook symptoms or delay screenings under the false belief that this disease belongs only to an older generation. The reality is far different: breast cancer does not discriminate by age, and complacency can have devastating consequences. It was precisely this recognition that motivated me, in my role as Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation, to take action—not only to educate myself about the disease, but also to help share vital knowledge with women everywhere.

When I first accepted this responsibility, I understood how much I had to learn. Like so many others, I harbored misconceptions about who was vulnerable and what could be done to protect against the disease. The more I studied, the clearer it became that awareness itself is one of the most powerful tools we possess. Knowledge dispels fear, replaces myth with fact, and empowers women to become active participants in their own health.

Of all the lessons I have absorbed, none is more important than this: early detection is the single most critical factor in surviving breast cancer. The statistics speak for themselves. When breast cancer is caught early—before it has the chance to spread beyond its original site—the five-year survival rate rises to an extraordinary 97 percent. That figure represents countless lives saved, families kept whole, and futures preserved simply because the disease was identified in time.

This is why I urge every woman to make her health a priority. Regular self-examinations are essential, allowing women to become familiar with their own bodies and to notice any changes as soon as they occur. Equally important is maintaining open, honest communication with your doctor. No concern is too small to mention, and no question should go unasked. By combining vigilance at home with professional medical guidance, women give themselves the best possible chance of catching this disease at its most treatable stage.

The message is clear and hopeful: breast cancer can be beaten, but only if we remain informed, proactive, and unafraid to act. Together, through education and early detection, we can save lives.

# Editor's Note

When Reese first submitted the manuscript to our office, none of us could have predicted the response it would receive. As the senior editor, I felt it was important to include this brief note before you begin reading, to offer some context about the work and its remarkable author.

Reese arrived at our publishing house with little more than a battered notebook and an unshakable determination. I remember the day the note landed on my desk—a handwritten message paperclipped to the first chapter, apologizing for the coffee stains and explaining that this story had been written over the course of seven years, mostly in the quiet hours before dawn.

As an editor, I read hundreds of submissions each year. Most blend together, forgettable and formulaic. But Reese's voice was different. There was an honesty in the prose that resisted every attempt I made to polish it into something more conventional. Time and again, I would suggest a revision, only to receive a thoughtful note in return, gently but firmly defending the original choice. I came to respect that stubbornness. It was, I realized, the very thing that made the work worth publishing.

This note is my small tribute to a collaboration that changed how I understand my role. An editor's job is not to reshape a writer into someone else, but to help them become more fully themselves. Reese taught me that lesson better than anyone.

I hope you find, in the pages that follow, the same spark that first caught my attention. Read slowly. Pay attention to the quiet moments. And remember that behind every published book stands a writer who dared to send their words into the world—and an editor lucky enough to receive them.

*— The Editor*

# I Know the Power of Early Detection. That's Why I'm Fighting for Every Woman.

*Editor's Note: Reese Witherspoon is an Academy Award-winning actress and producer. She serves as Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation for Women, where she advocates for breast cancer research and access to care. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author.*

---

When I was a little girl in Nashville, my mother, Betty, worked as a nurse. She spent her days caring for others, and around our dinner table, health was never a taboo subject. She taught me something I've carried my entire life: knowledge saves lives. Nowhere is that truer than in the fight against breast cancer.

Today, I have the profound honor of serving as the Avon Foundation for Women's Honorary Chair. It's a role I don't take lightly, because behind every statistic is a woman — a mother, a daughter, a sister, a friend — whose story deserves to continue.

## The Numbers Tell a Story We Can Change

Let me share why early detection matters so much.

When breast cancer is caught early — while it's still localized and hasn't spread beyond the breast — the five-year survival rate is approximately **99 percent**. Ninety-nine percent. That number should give every one of us hope.

But when the disease is diagnosed at a later stage, after it has spread to distant parts of the body, that survival rate drops dramatically — to around **30 percent**.

The difference between those two numbers is time. It's a mammogram scheduled instead of postponed. It's a self-exam that catches something new. It's access to a doctor who listens.

Consider this: roughly **1 in 8 women** in the United States will develop invasive breast cancer over the course of her lifetime. This year alone, hundreds of thousands of women will hear the words "you have breast cancer." Many of them will be caught early. Too many will not — and often, that gap comes down to who has access to care and who doesn't.

## This Fight Isn't Equal — And That Has to Change

Here's what keeps me up at night. Early detection only works if a woman can actually get screened. And for millions of women — those without insurance, those in rural communities, those juggling multiple jobs and childcare — a mammogram can feel like a luxury they simply cannot afford.

That's exactly the injustice the Avon Foundation works to correct. Through breast health programs, mobile screening units, and financial support for underserved communities, we're working to make sure a woman's zip code or bank account doesn't determine whether she lives or dies.

We've helped fund research into better treatments. We've supported programs that bring free and low-cost screenings directly to the women who need them most. And we've stood beside survivors as they've rebuilt their lives.

## What You Can Do Today

You don't have to be an honorary chair to make a difference. Here's what I'm asking of you:

**Know your body.** Pay attention to changes, and don't dismiss them. You are your own best advocate.

**Talk to your doctor about screening.** Ask when you should begin mammograms based on your personal and family history.

**Check on the women you love.** Remind your mother, your sister, your best friend to schedule that appointment. A simple text could save a life.

**Show up for those who can't.** Support the organizations working to close the access gap, so that early detection becomes a reality for every woman, not just those who can afford it.

## Why I'll Never Stop

My mother taught me that caring for others is the highest calling. Every time I meet a survivor — every time I hear a story of a woman who caught it early and is now watching her children grow up — I'm reminded of why this work matters.

Breast cancer doesn't care how famous you are, how much money you make, or where you come from. But the outcome? That we can influence. Early detection is one of the most powerful tools we have, and it's within our reach.

So let's use it. Let's make sure every woman knows her worth, knows her body, and knows she has a community fighting for her.

Because when we catch it early, we don't just save lives. We save futures.

---

*If you or someone you love needs information about breast health screenings, talk to your healthcare provider or contact a local breast cancer organization to learn about resources in your community.*

# Don't Wait for a Reason: Why Every Woman Should Take Breast Cancer Seriously

*A personal commentary*

When I was in my twenties, I thought I was invincible. Breast cancer? That was something I associated with older women, with statistics that didn't apply to someone my age. I couldn't have been more wrong—and I'm sharing this because I don't want another young woman to make the same assumption I did.

**The Myth That Puts Us at Risk**

There's a dangerous belief circulating among young women: that we're too young to worry about breast cancer. I understand where it comes from. We're busy building careers, raising families, chasing dreams. Our health can feel like something to deal with "later."

But breast cancer doesn't check your ID. While it's true that risk increases with age, thousands of women under 40 are diagnosed every year. Younger women often face more aggressive forms of the disease, and because we're not thinking about it, we're less likely to catch it early. That delay can cost us everything.

**Knowledge Is Power**

Here's what I've learned, and what I wish someone had told me sooner:

- **Know your body.** Perform regular self-exams and pay attention to changes. You are your own first line of defense.
- **Know your family history.** If breast cancer runs in your family, talk to your doctor about earlier and more frequent screening.
- **Don't dismiss your instincts.** If something feels wrong, advocate for yourself. Ask questions. Demand answers.
- **Talk about it.** The more we share our stories, the more we break the silence that keeps women uninformed and afraid.

**Why I Walk**

This is why I'm proud to support the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer. It's more than a fundraiser—it's a movement. Every step raises money for research, screening, and treatment for those who need it most, including women who couldn't otherwise afford care.

When you join the Avon Walk, you're not just walking for yourself. You're walking for your mother, your sister, your daughter, your best friend—for every woman who has faced this diagnosis and every woman we can protect from facing it alone.

**Take the First Step Today**

I'm asking you to do two things. First, commit to your own health—schedule that appointment, do that self-exam, have that conversation with your doctor. Second, join me at the Avon Walk. Lace up your shoes, gather your friends, and be part of something bigger than yourself.

We can't control everything about this disease. But we *can* control how informed we are, how early we act, and how loudly we fight. Let's make sure no woman ever thinks she's too young to matter.

I'll see you at the starting line.

---

*To learn more or register for the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer, visit the official website.*

---

# The Lump I Almost Ignored

I've played women who were fearless. Warriors, queens, mothers who moved mountains for their children. But the bravest thing I ever did wasn't on any screen. It was picking up the phone to schedule a mammogram I'd been putting off for months.

I'm writing this not as the person you might recognize from magazine covers or awards shows, but as a woman who found a lump in the shower one ordinary Tuesday and spent the next seventy-two hours convinced my life was over.

It wasn't. Mine was benign. But that terrifying wait taught me something I've never forgotten: too many women don't get my ending, and far too often, it's because we're not talking about this loudly enough.

## The Numbers We Need to Face

Let me share what I've learned, because knowledge is the thing that saves lives.

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women worldwide. In the United States alone, roughly one in eight women will develop invasive breast cancer over the course of her lifetime. Sit with that number for a moment. Think of eight women you love. Your mother. Your sister. Your best friend since childhood.

But here is the number that should give us hope, and fire: when breast cancer is caught early, before it spreads beyond the breast, the five-year relative survival rate is around 99 percent. Ninety-nine percent. That is the power of early detection. That is what a mammogram, a self-exam, a single honest conversation with your doctor can do.

Compare that to breast cancer discovered after it has spread to distant parts of the body, where the five-year survival rate drops to roughly 30 percent. The difference between those numbers isn't luck. So often, it's *time*. It's awareness. It's a woman who knew her own body well enough to say, "Something is different."

## What I'm Asking You to Do

**Know your body.** Perform regular self-exams. You don't need medical training to notice a change—a lump, a thickening, dimpling of the skin, a difference in size or shape. You are the world's foremost expert on what "normal" feels like for you.

**Get screened.** Talk to your doctor about when mammograms make sense for you, especially if you have a family history. Don't do what I did and let fear turn into delay. Fear is exactly why we must act, not wait.

**Talk about it.** Break the silence. The women in my life who survived did so, in part, because someone before them was brave enough to share her story. Be that someone.

## Why We Cannot Stop at Awareness

Awareness saves lives today, but research saves the futures we haven't met yet. Every dollar directed toward breast cancer research brings us closer to better treatments, earlier detection tools, and one day—I truly believe this—a cure.

I've seen what advocacy can build. Decades ago, a breast cancer diagnosis was often whispered, hidden, endured in shame and isolation. Today, survival rates have climbed steadily, and much of that progress traces back to people who refused to be quiet. Who marched, funded, researched, and fought.

I want to be part of that legacy. I want *you* to be part of it too.

## A Personal Promise

I have used my voice to bring characters to life. Now I want to use it for something that matters far more than any role I'll ever play.

So here is my promise: I will keep talking about this, even when it's uncomfortable, even when it's frightening. And here is my ask of you: schedule the appointment. Do the self-exam. Have the conversation with the woman you love who keeps putting it off.

The lump I almost ignored could have been the story that ended everything. Instead, it became the story that changed how I use my platform.

Don't wait for your own terrifying Tuesday. The 99 percent are counting on you to catch it early. And the cure we're all reaching for is counting on us to keep fighting until we find it.

With love and unshakable hope,

*A grateful survivor of the scare—and an advocate for life*

---

*Note: This is a fictional persuasive essay written from the perspective of an unnamed actress. Statistics reflect widely reported figures; readers should consult current data from organizations like the American Cancer Society and speak with their healthcare providers about personal screening recommendations.*

# The Fight That Binds Us: A Mother, A Daughter, and the Promise of Tomorrow

There is a particular kind of silence that falls over a family when the word "cancer" enters the room. I remember it vividly—the way my mother's face changed, the way the afternoon light seemed to dim, the way time itself seemed to hold its breath. I was young, but old enough to understand that something had shifted permanently in our world.

That was the day breast cancer stopped being a statistic to me and became personal. It became my mother.

## A Diagnosis, A Turning Point

My mother faced her diagnosis the way she faced everything in life: with a fierce determination that I now recognize as one of her greatest gifts to me. She refused to let fear dictate her days. Instead, she educated herself, asked hard questions, and demanded to be a partner in her own care rather than a passive patient.

What I witnessed during those difficult months was not just a woman fighting for her life—it was a woman fighting for her future, for our family, and, though she couldn't have known it then, for a cause that would come to define my own life's work.

## Turning Pain Into Purpose

When you watch someone you love battle this disease, you're left with a choice. You can be swallowed by helplessness, or you can channel that raw energy into action. I chose action.

Getting involved with a major breast cancer foundation gave my grief and my gratitude somewhere to go. It connected me to a community of survivors, caregivers, researchers, and advocates who understood—without explanation—the particular weight I carried. Together, we became something more powerful than any of us could be alone.

Through this work, I've learned that fighting breast cancer happens on many fronts:

- **In the laboratory**, where brilliant researchers pursue breakthroughs that would have been unimaginable when my mother was first diagnosed.
- **In the clinic**, where early detection saves lives every single day.
- **In our communities**, where we ensure that no woman is left behind because of where she lives, what she earns, or the color of her skin.
- **In our conversations**, where breaking the silence and stigma can encourage someone to schedule that mammogram they've been putting off.

## The Progress We've Made—And the Miles to Go

I am filled with hope when I consider how far we've come. Survival rates have climbed dramatically. Treatments have become more targeted, more effective, and less brutal. What was once a near-certain death sentence has, for many, become a survivable—even manageable—diagnosis.

But hope is not the same as complacency.

Every year, hundreds of thousands of women hear the words my mother heard. Too many of them face this fight without adequate resources, without access to quality care, without the support system that helped carry my mother through. The disparities in outcomes—particularly for women of color and those in underserved communities—remain a moral urgency we cannot ignore.

This is why the fight continues. This is why the work matters.

## What My Mother Taught Me

My mother taught me that courage isn't the absence of fear—it's the decision that something else is more important than that fear. She taught me that our darkest moments can plant the seeds of our greatest purpose. And she taught me that we are never truly alone as long as we refuse to let each other be.

Today, when I stand alongside survivors and advocates, when I meet the families just beginning their own journeys, I see my mother in all of them. I see her strength, her humor, her refusal to give up. And I am reminded of why I do this work.

## An Invitation to Join the Fight

To anyone reading this: you have a role to play. Schedule your screening. Support a friend through her treatment. Donate what you can. Volunteer your time. Advocate for research funding and equitable care. Share your story, because your voice might be the one that saves a life.

We are writing the final chapters of breast cancer's story—a story that will one day end not in loss, but in a cure. My mother's fight became my fight. Now I'm asking you to make it yours, too.

Because the greatest tribute we can pay to those we've loved and those we've lost is to ensure that future generations of mothers and daughters get to grow old together.

That is the world we are fighting for. And together, we will win it.

---

# Every Three Minutes, a Woman Is Diagnosed

Every three minutes, a woman in this country hears the words that change everything: *You have breast cancer.* In the time it takes to read this article, several more women will join a sisterhood no one asks to be part of—daughters, mothers, sisters, friends, and neighbors whose lives will pivot on a single diagnosis.

But here is the truth we must hold onto alongside that sobering statistic: breast cancer is one of the most treatable cancers when it is caught early. And that changes everything, too.

## Early Detection Saves Lives

When breast cancer is found in its earliest, most localized stage, the five-year survival rate is remarkably high. The difference between a cancer caught early and one caught late can be the difference between a straightforward treatment and a long, grueling fight. It can be the difference between watching your children grow up and leaving them too soon.

This is why detection matters so deeply. Not as a source of fear, but as a source of power.

## Know Your Body

You know your body better than anyone. Pay attention to it. Familiarize yourself with how your breasts normally look and feel, so you can notice when something changes. Be alert to:

- A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm
- Changes in size, shape, or contour
- Skin dimpling, puckering, or redness
- Nipple discharge, especially if bloody
- Persistent pain in one spot

A change does not mean cancer—most breast changes are not cancer at all. But every change deserves attention, and none should be ignored out of fear or the hope that it will simply go away.

## Talk to Your Doctor

If you take one action after reading this, let it be this: **make the call.**

Talk to your doctor about your personal risk factors, including your family history. Ask when you should begin regular mammograms and how often you should have them. Guidelines vary, and your individual risk may mean a different schedule than someone else's. This is a conversation only you and your healthcare provider can have.

If you've been putting off a screening—because you're busy, because you're scared, because life keeps getting in the way—please, stop putting it off. That appointment on your to-do list could be the most important thing you do all year.

## To the Woman Reading This

Maybe you're overdue for a mammogram. Maybe you've noticed something and told yourself it's nothing. Maybe you're healthy and simply haven't thought much about it at all.

Wherever you are, this is your invitation to take action. Schedule the screening. Ask the questions. Speak up about the change you noticed. Encourage the women you love to do the same—because sometimes the reminder that saves a life comes from a friend, not a headline.

Every three minutes, a woman is diagnosed. Let's make sure that as many of those women as possible are diagnosed early, treated successfully, and given every chance to keep living the full, beautiful lives they deserve.

**Your health is worth the appointment. Make the call today.**
